title: Haram
description: Arabic term for religiously forbidden in Islam
wiki_lead:
Haram ( ; Arabic: حَرَام ḥarām [ħɑˈrɑːm]) is an Arabic term meaning sinful or prohibited. 
This may refer to either something sacred to which access is not allowed to the people who are not in a state of purity or who are not initiated into the sacred knowledge; or, in direct contrast, to an evil and thus "sinful action that is forbidden to be done". 
The term also denotes something "set aside", thus being the Arabic equivalent of the Hebrew concept חרם (ḥērem) and the concept of sacer (cf. sacred) in Roman law and religion. In Islamic jurisprudence, haram is used to refer to any act that is forbidden by Allah and is one of the five Islamic commandments (الأحكام الخمسة al-ʾAḥkām al-Ḵamsa) that define the morality of human action.
Acts that are haram are typically prohibited in the religious texts of the Quran and the sunnah category of haram is the highest status of prohibition. Something that is considered haram remains prohibited no matter how good the intention is or how honorable the purpose is. Sins, good, and meritorious acts are placed on the mizan (weighing scales) on the Day of Judgement and are weighed according to the sincerity of the doer. 
Views of different madhhabs or legal schools of thought can vary significantly regarding what is or is not haram based on the scholarly interpretation of the core religious texts (Quran and hadith).

Haram ( ; Arabic: حَرَام ḥarām [ħɑˈrɑːm]) is an Arabic term meaning sinful or prohibited. 
This may refer to either something sacred to which access is not allowed to the people who are not in a state of purity or who are not initiated into the sacred knowledge; or, in direct contrast, to an evil and thus "sinful action that is forbidden to be done". 
The term also denotes something "set aside", thus being the Arabic equivalent of the Hebrew concept חרם (ḥērem) and the concept of sacer (cf. sacred) in Roman law and religion. In Islamic jurisprudence, haram is used to refer to any act that is forbidden by Allah and is one of the five Islamic commandments (الأحكام الخمسة al-ʾAḥkām al-Ḵamsa) that define the morality of human action.
Acts that are haram are typically prohibited in the religious texts of the Quran and the sunnah category of haram is the highest status of prohibition. Something that is considered haram remains prohibited no matter how good the intention is or how honorable the purpose is. Sins, good, and meritorious acts are placed on the mizan (weighing scales) on the Day of Judgement and are weighed according to the sincerity of the doer. 
Views of different madhhabs or legal schools of thought can vary significantly regarding what is or is not haram based on the scholarly interpretation of the core religious texts (Quran and hadith).


Overview
Actions that are haram result in harm one way or another and are therefore considered a sin if carried out by a Muslim.

They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about intoxicants and gambling. Say, “There is great evil in both, as well as some benefit for people—but the evil outweighs the benefit...”
By bringing up the word "benefit" as an opposite to "sin", verse 2:219 of the Quran clarifies that haram is that which is harmful, in opposition to that which brings benefit; therefore, sin is that which hurts others or oneself.
An Islamic principle related to haram is that if something is prohibited or forbidden, then anything that leads to it is also considered a haram act. A similar principle is that the sin of haram is not limited to the person who engages in the prohibited activity, but the sin also extends to others who support the person in the activity, whether it be material or moral support.
In the  principles of Islamic jurisprudence (Arabic: أصول الفقه, romanized: uṣūl al-fiqh), rulings governing actions fall into categories known as "the five rulings" (الأحكام الخمسة, al-aḥkām al-khamsa). 
It is a sin or a crime to perform a forbidden action or not to perform a mandatory action. Avoiding reprehensible acts and performing recommended acts is held to be subject of reward in the afterlife, while allowed actions entail no judgement from God.

Obligatory (واجب, wājib or فرض, farḍ);
Recommended (مُسْتَحَبّ, mustaḥabb or المندوب, mandūb);
Neutral, that is, not involving God's judgment (مباح, mubāḥ);
Disliked or reprehensible (مكروه, makrūh);
Forbidden (حَرَام, ḥarām or محظور, maḥzūr).
Islamic jurists disagree on whether the term halal covers the first two, three, or four of these categories.
The two types of haram are:

الحرام لذاته, al-ḥarām li-ḏātihi – Prohibited because of its essence and harm it causes to an individual
Adultery, murder, theft
الحرام لغيره, al-ḥarām li-ġayrihi – Prohibited because of external reasons that are not fundamentally harmful but are associated to something that is prohibited
Ill-gotten wealth obtained through sin. Examples include money earned through cheating, stealing, corruption, murder, and interest, or any means that involve harm to another human being. Also, a deal or sale during Friday's prayers (salat al-jumu'ah). It is prohibited in Islam for a Muslim to profit from such haram actions. Any believer who benefits from or lives off wealth obtained through haram is a sinner.
Prayer in a house, taken illegally.
The religious term haram, based on the Quran, is applied to:

Actions, such as cursing, fornication, murder, and disrespecting one's parents

grok_lead: Haram (Arabic: Ø­ÙØ±ÙØ§Ù, á¸¥arÄm) denotes any act, object, or conduct explicitly prohibited in Islam by divine ordinance, as established through textual evidence in the Quran and Sunnah, entailing potential punishment for commission and reward for abstention. In Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh), haram forms one of five categorical rulings (ahkam al-khamsah) alongside obligatory ( fard), recommended (mandub), permissible ( mubah), and disliked ( makruh), with prohibitions deriving directly from primary sources rather than mere scholarly consensus or analogy unless rooted therein. Linguistically, the term contrasts with halal (permissible), originating from pre-Islamic usage for sacred sanctuaries but repurposed in revelation to signify inviolable taboos aimed at preserving human welfare, intellect, and societal order. Core prohibitions encompass consumption of pork and its byproducts, intoxicants including alcohol, carrion, blood, and carnivorous animals not slaughtered via Islamic ritual ( dhabihah), as stipulated in Quran 5:3, which declares these "impure" and forbidden to preserve physical and spiritual purity. Usury (riba), gambling (maysir), adultery (zina), theft, murder, and false testimony rank among behavioral harams, with Quranic injunctions like 5:90 equating intoxicants and gambling to Satan's handiwork that sows enmity and diverts from remembrance of God. These rulings apply universally to Muslims. The concept of haram primarily applies to Muslims who believe in and follow Islam; non-Muslims are not bound by these specific obligations and prohibitions of Sharia in this life, though they may be subject to general public order laws under Islamic governance. with gradations in severityâsuch as hudud-prescribed penalties for certain crimes like theft or illicit sexâenforced variably across historical caliphates and modern states adhering to sharia, though empirical implementation has often prioritized deterrence over uniformity due to evidentiary thresholds like witness corroboration. Interpretive variances arise among the four Sunni madhahib (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali) and Shia traditions, yet all anchor haram in explicit nass (definitive texts) over qiyas (analogy) for unambiguous cases, cautioning against expansive prohibitions absent clear warrant to avoid burdening the faith beyond prophetic intent. Contemporary applications, such as deeming certain financial instruments or biotechnologies haram if involving riba or genetic alteration contravening creation's sanctity, reflect causal reasoning from foundational texts rather than cultural accretions, underscoring Islam's emphasis on outcomes like economic equity and health preservation over permissive modernism. Scholarly sources deriving from authenticated hadith collections, like Sahih al-Bukhari, maintain higher fidelity to original intent compared to secondary analyses prone to ideological overlay.
